title: AGENTS.md — scrutiny
text: scrutiny implements statistical error-detection techniques published summary statistics — primarily consistency tests GRIM, GRIMMER, DEBIT. also provides infrastructure (function factories) implementing new consistency tests. package tidyverse-oriented: tidy data, tibbles throughout (never data.frame()s), dplyr/purrr idioms.

title: DEBIT
text: explain_print() explains results debit_map() step step, GRIM GRIMMER. inconsistent value set pigs3: explain_map() adds explanations explanation column instead, debit_explain() explains single value set. default formula = "exact" can explained.
code: pigs3 |>   debit_map(digits_x = 2, digits_sd = 2, data_type = "integer") |>   dplyr::filter(!consistency) |>   explain_print() #> DEBIT test: x = 0.19, sd = 0.35, n = 1683, data_type = "integer" #>  #> DEBIT is about binary data, where every value is 0 or 1. The mean is then the #> share of ones, and the SD follows from the number of ones and the sample size. #>  #> The mean was reported as 0.19, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding (assuming #> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from #> 0.185 to 0.195. #>  #> With 1683 values, the mean is the number of ones divided by 1683, so that #> number must be from 0.185 * 1683 = 311.355 to 0.195 * 1683 = 328.185. It has to #> be an integer, so it can be anything from 312 to 328. #>  #> The SD was reported as 0.35, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding, it could #> have been anything from 0.345 to 0.355. #>  #> With k ones among 1683 values, the SD is sqrt(k * (1683 - k) / (1683 * 1682)). #> Even the smallest of these SDs, for k = 312, is #> sqrt(312 * 1371 / 2830806) = 0.3887, which is above that range. #>  #> ==> Inconsistent

title: GRIMMER basics
text: explain_print() explains results grimmer_map() step step, GRIM. inconsistent value set : explain_map() adds explanations explanation column instead, grimmer_explain() explains single value set. see test rather read , draw one value set grimmer_plot_line(); see vignette("grimmer--depth").
code: flying_pigs1 |>   grimmer_map(digits_x = 1, digits_sd = 2, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer") |>   dplyr::filter(!consistency) |>   explain_print() #> GRIMMER test: x = 2.6, sd = 2.05, n = 25, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer" #>  #> The mean was reported as 2.6, with 1 decimal place. Before rounding (assuming #> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from #> 2.55 to 2.65. #>  #> The mean of 25 integers is their sum divided by 25. So the sum must be from #> 2.55 * 25 = 63.75 to 2.65 * 25 = 66.25. #>  #> A sum of integers is itself an integer, and the integers from 64 to 66 are in #> this range. For example, 65 / 25 = 2.6, which rounds to 2.6. #>  #> The SD was reported as 2.05, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding, it could #> have been anything from 2.045 to 2.055. #>  #> Together, the sum and the SD determine the sum of squares, which is what you #> get by squaring each of the 25 values and adding them up. It is #> (25 - 1) * SD^2 + sum^2 / 25. The values are integers, so their squares are #> integers, too, and so is the sum of squares. What's more, an integer and its #> square are either both odd or both even. So the sum of squares must be odd if #> the sum is odd, and even if the sum is even. #>  #> With a sum of 64, the sum of squares is from #> 24 * 2.045^2 + 64^2 / 25 = 264.2086 to 24 * 2.055^2 + 64^2 / 25 = 265.1926. The #> only integer in this range is 265, which is odd, but 64 is even. #>  #> With a sum of 65, the sum of squares is from #> 24 * 2.045^2 + 65^2 / 25 = 269.3686 to 24 * 2.055^2 + 65^2 / 25 = 270.3526. The #> only integer in this range is 270, which is even, but 65 is odd. #>  #> With a sum of 66, the sum of squares is from #> 24 * 2.045^2 + 66^2 / 25 = 274.6086 to 24 * 2.055^2 + 66^2 / 25 = 275.5926. The #> only integer in this range is 275, which is odd, but 66 is even. #>  #> ==> Inconsistent

code: debit_explain(   x = 0.36,   sd = 0.11,   n = 20,   digits_x = 2,   digits_sd = 2,   data_type = "integer" ) #> DEBIT test: x = 0.36, sd = 0.11, n = 20, data_type = "integer" #>  #> DEBIT is about binary data, where every value is 0 or 1. The mean is then the #> share of ones, and the SD follows from the number of ones and the sample size. #>  #> The mean was reported as 0.36, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding (assuming #> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from #> 0.355 to 0.365. #>  #> With 20 values, the mean is the number of ones divided by 20, so that number #> must be from 0.355 * 20 = 7.1 to 0.365 * 20 = 7.3. But it has to be an integer, #> and there is none in this range. So no number of ones fits the mean, whatever #> the SD is. #>  #> ==> Inconsistent  debit_explain(   x = 0.35,   sd = 0.49,   n = 20,   digits_x = 2,   digits_sd = 2,   data_type = "integer" ) #> DEBIT test: x = 0.35, sd = 0.49, n = 20, data_type = "integer" #>  #> DEBIT is about binary data, where every value is 0 or 1. The mean is then the #> share of ones, and the SD follows from the number of ones and the sample size. #>  #> The mean was reported as 0.35, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding (assuming #> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from #> 0.345 to 0.355. #>  #> With 20 values, the mean is the number of ones divided by 20, so that number #> must be from 0.345 * 20 = 6.9 to 0.355 * 20 = 7.1. It has to be an integer, so #> it can only be 7. #>  #> The SD was reported as 0.49, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding, it could #> have been anything from 0.485 to 0.495. #>  #> With k ones among 20 values, the SD is sqrt(k * (20 - k) / (20 * 19)). For #> k = 7, that is sqrt(7 * 13 / 380) = 0.4894, which is in that range. #>  #> ==> Consistent

title: Explain a GRIM test step by step — grim_explain
code: grim_explain(   x = 5.19,   n = 28,   digits_x = 2,   items_averaged = 1,   data_type = "integer" ) #> GRIM test: x = 5.19, n = 28, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer" #>  #> The mean was reported as 5.19, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding (assuming #> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from #> 5.185 to 5.195. #>  #> The mean of 28 integers is their sum divided by 28. So the sum must be from #> 5.185 * 28 = 145.18 to 5.195 * 28 = 145.46. #>  #> A sum of integers is itself an integer, but there is no integer in this range. #> The nearest ones are 145 and 146. They give 145 / 28 = 5.1786 and #> 146 / 28 = 5.2143, which round to 5.18 and 5.21, not to 5.19. #>  #> ==> Inconsistent  grim_explain(   x = 5.19,   n = 32,   digits_x = 2,   items_averaged = 1,   data_type = "integer" ) #> GRIM test: x = 5.19, n = 32, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer" #>  #> The mean was reported as 5.19, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding (assuming #> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from #> 5.185 to 5.195. #>  #> The mean of 32 integers is their sum divided by 32. So the sum must be from #> 5.185 * 32 = 165.92 to 5.195 * 32 = 166.24. #>  #> A sum of integers is itself an integer, and 166 is in this range: #> 166 / 32 = 5.1875, which rounds to 5.19. #>  #> ==> Consistent  grim_explain(   x = 71,   n = 43,   digits_x = 0,   items_averaged = 1,   data_type = "integer",   x_meaning = "percentage" ) #> GRIM test: x = 71, n = 43, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer", x_meaning = "percentage" #>  #> The percentage was reported as 71%, with no decimal places. Before rounding #> (assuming either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been #> anything from 70.5% to 71.5%. #>  #> A percentage out of 43 is a count divided by 43, times 100. So 71% stands for #> the proportion 0.71, with two more decimal places than the percentage shows. #> The count must be from 70.5 / 100 * 43 = 30.315 to 71.5 / 100 * 43 = 30.745. #>  #> A count is an integer, but there is no integer in this range. The nearest ones #> are 30 and 31. They give 30 / 43 * 100 = 69.7674 and 31 / 43 * 100 = 72.093, #> which round to 70% and 72%, not to 71%. #>  #> ==> Inconsistent

title: Explain a GRIMMER test step by step — grimmer_explain
code: grimmer_explain(   x = 5.23,   sd = 2.55,   n = 35,   digits_x = 2,   digits_sd = 2,   items_averaged = 1,   data_type = "integer" ) #> GRIMMER test: x = 5.23, sd = 2.55, n = 35, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer" #>  #> The mean was reported as 5.23, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding (assuming #> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from #> 5.225 to 5.235. #>  #> The mean of 35 integers is their sum divided by 35. So the sum must be from #> 5.225 * 35 = 182.875 to 5.235 * 35 = 183.225. #>  #> A sum of integers is itself an integer, and 183 is in this range: #> 183 / 35 = 5.2286, which rounds to 5.23. #>  #> The SD was reported as 2.55, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding, it could #> have been anything from 2.545 to 2.555. #>  #> Together, the sum and the SD determine the sum of squares, which is what you #> get by squaring each of the 35 values and adding them up. It is #> (35 - 1) * SD^2 + sum^2 / 35. The values are integers, so their squares are #> integers, too, and so is the sum of squares. What's more, an integer and its #> square are either both odd or both even. So the sum of squares must be odd if #> the sum is odd, and even if the sum is even. #>  #> With a sum of 183, the sum of squares is from #> 34 * 2.545^2 + 183^2 / 35 = 1177.0474 to 34 * 2.555^2 + 183^2 / 35 = 1178.7814. #> The only integer in this range is 1178, which is even, but 183 is odd. #>  #> ==> Inconsistent  grimmer_explain(   x = 5.23,   sd = 2.55,   n = 31,   digits_x = 2,   digits_sd = 2,   items_averaged = 1,   data_type = "integer" ) #> GRIMMER test: x = 5.23, sd = 2.55, n = 31, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer" #>  #> The mean was reported as 5.23, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding (assuming #> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from #> 5.225 to 5.235. #>  #> The mean of 31 integers is their sum divided by 31. So the sum must be from #> 5.225 * 31 = 161.975 to 5.235 * 31 = 162.285. #>  #> A sum of integers is itself an integer, and 162 is in this range: #> 162 / 31 = 5.2258, which rounds to 5.23. #>  #> The SD was reported as 2.55, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding, it could #> have been anything from 2.545 to 2.555. #>  #> Together, the sum and the SD determine the sum of squares, which is what you #> get by squaring each of the 31 values and adding them up. It is #> (31 - 1) * SD^2 + sum^2 / 31. The values are integers, so their squares are #> integers, too, and so is the sum of squares. What's more, an integer and its #> square are either both odd or both even. So the sum of squares must be odd if #> the sum is odd, and even if the sum is even. #>  #> With a sum of 162, the sum of squares is from #> 30 * 2.545^2 + 162^2 / 31 = 1040.8914 to 30 * 2.555^2 + 162^2 / 31 = 1042.4214. #> The integers from 1041 to 1042 are in this range, so one of them is even, like #> 162. #>  #> ==> Consistent

So the sum must be from #> 7.215 * 38 = 274.17 to 7.225 * 38 = 274.55. #>  #> A sum of integers is itself an integer, but there is no integer in this range. #> The nearest ones are 274 and 275. They give 274 / 38 = 7.2105 and #> 275 / 38 = 7.2368, which round to 7.21 and 7.24, not to 7.22. So the sum of squares must be odd if #> the sum is odd, and even if the sum is even. #>  #> With a sum of 147, the sum of squares is from #> 30 * 6.545^2 + 147^2 / 31 = 1982.1753 to 30 * 6.555^2 + 147^2 / 31 = 1986.1053. #> The integers from 1983 to 1986 are in this range, so one of them is odd, like #> 147. #>  #> ==> Consistent #>
